name: Cache/timing side-channel attack analysis and constant-time fix
identify_givens: A stated cache geometry (total size, number of lines, bytes per line, direct-mapped, data cache only), an array/table layout saying which entries map to which cache line, a short C-like victim program with secret variables (e.g. A, B, C) and possibly an attacker-controlled public input (e.g. D), and an attacker model: time-driven (execution time depends only on number of cache misses/hits) or access-driven (attacker observes which cache lines are touched/evicted, possibly over repeated runs with chosen inputs).
identify_target: Explain why the program is insecure and name the leaking instructions; show how the attacker correlates multiple executions (varying the public input) to recover a secret value, range, or predicate; propose a concrete fix (constant-time/branchless rewrite or cache preloading/flushing); and sometimes judge whether speculative execution (branch prediction) increases the leakage.
strategy_name: Map lines, flag secret-dependent accesses, correlate runs, then make the footprint secret-independent

algorithm.detail: From the geometry compute the line of every datum: entry $i$ of an array with 4-byte entries and $L$-byte lines sits in line $\lfloor i \cdot 4 / L \rfloor \bmod N_{lines}$. Note collisions: two arrays (or two regions) mapping to the same line evict each other, so only one can be cached at a time.

Mark every instruction whose memory index, branch condition, or iteration count depends on a secret (directly, or mixed with attacker input, e.g. $M[(B+D) \bmod 64]$). These are the only possible leak sources; accesses with public/constant indices never leak.

Time-driven: count cache misses per execution, simulating the direct-mapped cache line by line (a miss occurs when the needed line differs from the currently resident one). Access-driven: assume the attacker flushes/primes the cache before the run and records the set of lines touched (or evicted) after it.

Enumerate the attacker-controlled input values and tabulate the observed line set or miss count for each. Subtract the parts the attacker already knows (constant lines, lines of public indices like $\lfloor D/16 \rfloor$); the remaining variation is a function of the secret, e.g. observing line $((B+D) \bmod 64)/16$ while sweeping $D$ pins down $B$. State precisely what is recovered: exact value, a range, or one bit (predicate true/false).

Match the fix to the leak source: for secret-dependent branches/indices use constant-time code — fixed loop bounds, always execute both sides, select with arithmetic $r = b \cdot x + (1-b) \cdot y$, secret-independent indices; for secret-dependent array indices use cache priming — preload (or flush) all possibly-used lines first, e.g. read $M[0], M[16], M[32], M[48]$, so the cache footprint is identical for every secret.

Under branch prediction, instructions on a mispredicted path may execute transiently and still fetch their lines into the cache (a speculative reading gadget, possibly an overread if the index is unbounded). But leakage additionally needs a transmitter (a way to encode the loaded value into the cache state); a reading gadget alone discloses nothing extra. Conclude whether speculation adds leakage.

variations.name: Time-driven vs access-driven on the same program
variations.detail: The professor swaps the attacker model and the answer flips. Under time-driven counting, colliding arrays can make the miss count constant for straight-line code (trap: do not claim leakage there), while a secret-dependent branch still leaks one bit via one extra miss. Under access-driven observation with no shared memory, the same program may leak nothing because the same lines are always evicted; with shared memory the attacker can tell which array is resident. Always redo Step 3 for the stated model instead of reusing conclusions.

variations.name: Single-run boolean leak vs multi-run exact recovery
variations.detail: Sometimes there is no attacker input (dasak18: only secrets A, B, C) — then one execution leaks at most a predicate (e.g. B true causes one extra miss). When the attacker controls an input D and may rerun (exam P8), the secret-dependent index $(B+D) \bmod 64$ sweeps across lines as D varies, upgrading the leak from a range to the exact value of B. Adapt Step 4: without a knob, tabulate the two branch cases; with a knob, sweep all its values.

variations.name: Wrong-fix trap: branchless vs preloading
variations.detail: The fix must match the flagged instruction from Step 2. A branchless select $a \mathrel{+}= B \cdot A_1 + (1-B) \cdot A_2$ fixes a secret-dependent branch but does nothing for a secret-dependent array index; preloading all lines $M[0], M[16], M[32], M[48]$ fixes index leakage but not a secret-dependent loop bound. Answers proposing the mismatched fix lose points.

variations.name: Speculation sub-question with gadget reasoning
variations.detail: A final part asks whether speculative execution leaks more. The expected reasoning is two-part: transient loads on a mispredicted path can fill lines (and an unbounded index like $M[D]$ with $D \geq 64$ is a speculative overread, unlike the $\bmod\,64$-guarded one), but without a speculative transmitter no extra information is disclosed. Trap: answering 'Spectre, so yes it leaks' without identifying reading gadget vs transmitter.

example_problem: A system has a direct-mapped data cache (no instruction cache) of 512 bytes, 8 lines, 64 bytes per line. Array M has 64 entries of 4 bytes; entries 0-15 map to line 0, 16-31 to line 1, 32-47 to line 2, 48-63 to line 3. M is public with M[i] = i. A, B, C are secret (A < 64); D is public and attacker-controlled; A, B, C, D share one 64-byte block on line 4 (fifth line). Victim program: (1) C = 0; (2) C += M[A]; (3) if (D < 64) { (4) C += M[D]; (5) C += M[(B + D) mod 64]; }. The attacker runs an access-driven attack: he observes which cache lines are accessed at least once per execution, over multiple executions with the same A, B, C and all values of D. (8a) Explain why the program is not secure and which instructions leak. (8b) Explain how the attacker correlates executions to learn the initial secret values.

example_steps.work: Line size 64 B and 4-byte entries give 16 entries per line, so $M[i]$ sits in line $\lfloor i/16 \rfloor$ for $i < 64$; A, B, C, D all sit together on line 4. No array-internal collisions beyond this partitioning.

Line 2 ($C \mathrel{+}= M[A]$) has an index depending directly on secret A, and line 5 ($C \mathrel{+}= M[(B+D) \bmod 64]$) has an index depending on secret B and attacker input D. Per the official solution, lines 2 and 5 are exactly the leaking instructions; line 4 uses only public D.

Access-driven model: before each run the attacker flushes the data cache and records which lines are filled after execution. When $D < 64$ the program accesses lines $\lfloor A/16 \rfloor$, $\lfloor D/16 \rfloor$, and $\lfloor ((D+B) \bmod 64)/16 \rfloor$ (plus the constant line 4 of the scalar variables).

Correlate over runs: with $A = B = D = 0$ only the first cache line is accessed; with $A = B = 16,\ D = 0$ only the second cache line is accessed. Since $\lfloor A/16 \rfloor$ is constant across runs and $\lfloor D/16 \rfloor$ is known to the attacker, the varying third line reveals $(B+D) \bmod 64$; by varying $D$ over all values the attacker sweeps this index across the lines and, per the official solution, identifies the exact value of B (while A is narrowed to its line, 16 candidates).

Official fix (8c): cache flush or prefetch — preload or flush all cache lines before use so timing/footprint does not reveal which one was actually needed; concretely, read $M[0], M[16], M[32], M[48]$ at the beginning of the program so every line of M is resident regardless of A and B.

Official answer (8d): with branch prediction the loads $M[D]$ and $M[(B+D) \bmod 64]$ may execute speculatively even when $D \geq 64$; only the first is a speculative overread since the second is guarded by mod. Both give a speculative reading gadget but there is no speculative transmitter, so no additional information is disclosed.
